title: Blood transfusion and iron overload
covers: Blood components and blood groups, AABB red cell and platelet thresholds, leukocyte depletion and irradiation, safe transfusion practice, transfusion reactions and their treatment, and iron overload with hereditary hemochromatosis.

ul: Red cells are the most transfused component. Whole blood donation is spun into components; apheresis keeps one component and returns the rest.

ul: Red cell antigen: a sugar or protein on the red cell surface, defined by an antibody. Blood group system: ≥ 1 antigens controlled by one gene or closely linked genes (ISBT 2024: 366 antigens, 47 systems).
Phenotype = the antigens on the red cell surface (used to match chronic transfusions, e.g. sickle cell stroke). Genotype = the DNA sequence at the antigen loci.
Incompatible blood agglutinates and can kill. Typing is used for pretransfusion testing, transplantation, reaction workup and HDFN risk.

Typing: red cells + anti-A, anti-B, anti-Rh reagents; agglutination = that antigen is present.

Avoid platelets in TTP and HIT (platelet activation) except for life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedures.

ul: Before: identify patient and unit; ABO/Rh/antibody screen; cross-match; infection screen (HIV, HBV, HCV, HTLV); consent; good IV access.
Discard a unit at room temperature > 4 h, out of the fridge > 30 min, opened, or deteriorated.
Check the bag: seal, pink plasma (hemolysis), interface, leaks, clots, purple or black red cells. A failed bag goes back to the blood bank.
Red cells: standard filter; adults 1–2 mL/min for 15 min, then as tolerated, within 4 h; only 0.9% NaCl, ABO-compatible plasma or albumin in the line; no drugs.
Give the first 5 mL/kg quickly to relieve hypoxia, then slowly; diuretic if at risk of heart failure; monitor until 30 min after; reassess; a second 5–10 mL/kg if needed.
Platelets: plasma-compatible, ABO-identical preferred; red cell stroma can cause Rh immunization; finish within 30 min.

items.note: Case 6 (slide 32) is a boy with agammaglobulinemia given IVIG. Anti-IgA anaphylaxis needs a patient who can make anti-IgA (IgA deficiency); an agammaglobulinemic patient cannot. The reaction type was tested only with IgA deficiency. Slide 36 times FNHTR at 1–6 hours after transfusion; standard definitions use during or within 4 hours. Not tested.

ul: Prevention: a restrictive attitude to transfusion plus pretransfusion testing.
First step: stop the transfusion, keep the IV open with 0.9% NaCl, see the patient. Then stabilize, assess, confirm donor-recipient compatibility, call the primary team, blood bank and ICU.
Treat every acute reaction as potentially serious until proved otherwise: early benign and serious reactions look alike.

Stop permanently if: onset < 15 min, temperature > 39 °C, hypotension or shock, chills, back or chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia or arrhythmia, flushing or hives over > 2/3 of the body, hemoglobinuria, bleeding at the IV site.
From raised intake (transfusion) or raised gut absorption with normal intake. Symptoms are vague and slow, so it is often missed; untreated it causes irreversible organ damage and death.
Humans have a limited capacity to excrete iron, so chronic transfusion always leads to overload.

table: Transfusion-dependent thalassemia, sickle cell disease, severe hemolytic anemias, Fanconi, Diamond-Blackfan, MDS, aplastic anemia
Hereditary hemochromatosis; ineffective erythropoiesis (NTDT, sideroblastic anemia, CDA, MDS)

ul: The most common cause of severe iron overload. Autosomal recessive; HFE gene on the short arm of chromosome 6. C282Y homozygosity in ~80%; also C282Y/H63D and other HFE variants; non-HFE genes are rarer.
75% are asymptomatic, found on routine chemistry or family screening. Usual onset 40–50 years (juvenile form 10–30).

Manifestations: cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, endocrinopathies (diabetes), skin pigmentation, hepatocellular carcinoma, arthropathy. Classic triad: cirrhosis + diabetes + pigmentation ("bronze diabetes").
Labs: transferrin saturation ≥ 45%, ferritin ≥ 150–300 ng/mL without inflammation, high liver iron, C282Y homozygosity; ferritin normalizes with phlebotomy.

Treatment: remove iron before irreversible damage. Phlebotomy until iron depletion, chelation, liver transplant for end-stage liver disease or HCC, arthroplasty for destroyed joints. Early treatment improves survival.

items.note: Slide 49 lists a "neonatal form" of HH; neonatal hemochromatosis is usually a separate (alloimmune) disease. Slide 49 calls cirrhosis the most common manifestation. Neither was tested.

questions.stem: A volunteer donates one unit of whole blood for a trauma patient. Which of the following is NOT part of that unit as collected?
questions.explanation: Whole blood (500 mL) contains red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma. Cryoprecipitate is prepared later from plasma. A: Part of whole blood. B: Part of whole blood. C: Part of whole blood. D: Part of whole blood.

questions.stem: Which blood component is transfused most often?
questions.explanation: Transfusion of RBCs is the most common. A: Less often. C: Less often. D: Less often. E: Less often.

questions.stem: How does apheresis differ from whole blood donation?

options.B: The whole unit is spun into its components
options.C: Plasma is fractionated into clotting factors
options.D: Red cells are irradiated before storage
options.E: The donor gives a larger single volume

questions.explanation: Apheresis: one component (platelets, red cells or plasma) is collected and the rest returned to the donor. Whole blood: the unit is spun and separated into its components. B: Whole blood donation. C: Plasma processing. D: Processing, not collection. E: Not the difference.

questions.stem: Which product is prepared from donated plasma?
questions.explanation: Plasma gives fresh frozen plasma, prothrombin complex concentrate, cryoprecipitate, clotting factors, immunoglobulins and albumin. A: From whole blood or plateletpheresis. B: Red cell product. C: Cellular product. E: Red cell product.

questions.stem: How are apheresis platelets stored?
questions.explanation: Platelets: room temperature with agitation, given over 15–30 min. A: Red cells and whole blood. B: Fresh frozen plasma. D: Cryoprecipitate. E: Prothrombin complex concentrate.

questions.stem: A unit of packed red cells is issued from the blood bank. At what temperature is it stored?
questions.explanation: Whole blood and packed red cells: +1 to +6 °C, given within 4 hours. A: Platelets. C: Fresh frozen plasma. D: Cryoprecipitate. E: Prothrombin complex concentrate.

questions.stem: A man with liver failure and DIC has several low clotting factors and is bleeding. Which product fits?
questions.explanation: FFP (clotting factors, albumin, immunoglobulins; ≤ −25 °C; 30 min): DIC, liver failure, multiple clotting factor deficiencies. A: VWF, VIII, XIII deficiencies. B: Thrombocytopenia. C: No clotting factors. E: Immune cytopenia, immune deficiency.

questions.stem: A man on warfarin has an intracranial bleed. Which product gives rapid reversal?
questions.explanation: PCC (factors II, VII, IX, X, proteins C and S; slow IV push): life-threatening bleeding, rapid warfarin reversal. A: VWF, VIII, XIII. B: Not for warfarin reversal. C: No clotting factors. D: Not a factor product.

questions.stem: Which protein is present in prothrombin complex concentrate?
questions.explanation: PCC contains factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins S and C. Cryoprecipitate carries VIII, XIII and VWF. B: Cryoprecipitate. C: Cryoprecipitate. D: Cryoprecipitate. E: No concentrate exists.

questions.stem: A woman with von Willebrand disease bleeds during surgery, and no factor concentrate is available. Which blood component supplies VWF?
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate (10–20 mL; ≤ −18 °C): factor VIII, XIII and VWF deficiencies, trauma, DIC, unavailable factor concentrate. A: II, VII, IX, X. B: Not the VWF source. D: No clotting factors. E: No clotting factors.

questions.stem: For which factor is no clotting factor concentrate available?
questions.explanation: Clotting factor concentrates: all clotting factors except FV; used for disorders of secondary hemostasis. A: Concentrate exists. B: Concentrate exists. C: Concentrate exists. D: Concentrate exists.

questions.stem: Immunoglobulin products used for immune cytopenias are made mostly of which class?
questions.explanation: Immunoglobulins: mostly IgG; 2–6 °C; given over 3 h; immune cytopenia and immune deficiencies. A: Not the main class. B: Not the main class. D: Not the main class. E: Not the main class.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with sickle cell disease and a stroke starts chronic transfusion with phenotype-matched red cells. What is being matched?

options.A: All antigens on the red cell surface
options.B: The genetic sequences at the antigen loci
options.C: A group of antigens from one gene
options.D: A surface molecule defined by an antibody
options.E: The ABO and RhD group of the donor

questions.explanation: RBC phenotype: combination of antigens on the RBC surface. Genotype: genetic sequences at the loci for blood group antigens. B: Genotype. C: Blood group system. D: A red cell antigen. E: Part of the phenotype.

questions.stem: What is a blood group system?

options.A: The antigens on a person's red cells
options.B: Antigens from one gene or linked genes
options.C: DNA sequences at blood group loci
options.D: A surface sugar defined by an antibody
options.E: The antibodies found in a person's plasma

questions.explanation: Blood group system: a group of ≥ 1 antigens controlled by a single gene or a cluster of closely linked genes. ISBT 2024: 366 antigens, 47 systems. A: Phenotype. C: Genotype. D: A red cell antigen. E: Not the definition.

questions.stem: How many blood group systems does the ISBT list (2024)?
questions.explanation: ISBT working group 2024: 366 human red cell antigens and 47 blood group systems. A: Number of antigens. B: ABO and Rh groups. C: ABO groups. E: Not the value.

questions.stem: Besides pretransfusion testing, blood typing is used to assess the risk of which disease?
questions.explanation: Blood typing: pretransfusion testing, organ transplantation, evaluation of transfusion reactions and risk of HDFN. A: Membrane defect. B: Enzyme defect. C: Acquired clonal defect. D: Not assessed by typing.

questions.stem: The ABO genes are located on which chromosome?
questions.explanation: ABO: the most important blood group system; genes on chromosome 9; involved in severe hemolytic reactions and HDFN. A: HFE. C: β-globin. D: α-globin. E: Not ABO.

questions.stem: Which is the most important antigen of the Rh system?
questions.explanation: Rh is the 2nd most important system; major antigens D (most important), C, c, E, e. A: Major, less important. B: Major, less important. D: Minor system (Kell). E: Minor system (Duffy).

questions.stem: Which is a minor but clinically significant blood group system?
questions.explanation: Major systems: ABO and Rh. Minor clinically significant systems: Kell, Kidd, Duffy, MNS. A: Major system. B: Major system. C: Not a red cell system. E: Platelet antigens.

questions.stem: A patient's red cells agglutinate with anti-B and anti-Rh reagents but not with anti-A. What is the blood group?
questions.explanation: Agglutination means the red cells carry the antigen bound by the reagent antibody: B antigen and Rh antigen present, A absent. B: Would agglutinate with anti-A. C: Would agglutinate with anti-A. D: Would not agglutinate with anti-B. E: Would agglutinate with anti-A, not anti-Rh.

questions.stem: A woman is blood group O. Which antibodies are present in her plasma?
questions.explanation: If an antigen is on a person's red cells, the matching antibody is absent from plasma. Group O cells lack A and B, so plasma has anti-A and anti-B. A: Group B. B: Group A. D: Group AB. E: Not naturally present.

questions.stem: In an emergency with no time for typing, which red cells can be given to any recipient?
questions.explanation: O negative is the universal donor: no A, B or Rh (D) antigen on the red cells. B: Carries A and B antigens. C: Universal recipient type. D: Carries A antigen. E: Carries B antigen.

questions.stem: A stable 60-year-old inpatient with AML has Hb 7.4 g/dL, no bleeding and no heart disease. What is the best decision?
questions.explanation: AABB restrictive threshold: Hb < 7 g/dL for most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, including those with hematologic or oncologic disease. Decisions rest on the clinical context, not Hb alone. A: Above the restrictive threshold of 7. B: Above the threshold. C: Fresh units are not needed. D: No indication given.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with coronary artery disease is about to have major surgery. His Hb is 7.6 g/dL. What is the best decision?

options.A: Wait until Hb is below 7 g/dL

questions.explanation: Higher threshold, Hb < 8 g/dL, in selected patients with cardiovascular disease or undergoing major surgery. A: A higher threshold applies. B: Not for anemia. C: Not indicated. E: Not for anemia.

questions.stem: For most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, red cells are transfused below which hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Restrictive threshold: Hb < 7 g/dL for most stable hospitalized adults and critically ill but stable children; < 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or major surgery. A: Cardiovascular disease or major surgery. C: Too high. D: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A resident asks the blood bank for red cells stored less than 10 days for a stable inpatient with anemia. Which units are appropriate?
questions.explanation: RBC units can be used within their approved shelf life; fresh (< 10 days) units are not routinely necessary. A: Fresh units are not routinely necessary. B: Not advised. C: Not advised. D: Not advised.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with pre-B-cell ALL needs a lumbar puncture. Below what platelet count should platelets be given first?
questions.explanation: AABB: lumbar puncture, transfuse at < 20 ×10⁹/L. A: Major non-spine surgery. B: Prophylaxis during chemotherapy. D: Preterm neonates. E: Not a threshold.

questions.stem: A man receiving chemotherapy for AML has a platelet count of 12 ×10⁹/L and no bleeding. What is the best decision?
questions.explanation: Hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia on chemotherapy or allogeneic SCT without bleeding: transfuse at < 10 ×10⁹/L. A: Threshold is < 10. C: No indication. D: No indication. E: No bleeding.

questions.stem: A woman needs a major abdominal operation (not involving the spine). Platelets should be raised above what level?
questions.explanation: AABB: major surgery not involving the spine, transfuse at < 50 ×10⁹/L. A: Lumbar puncture. B: Prophylaxis on chemotherapy. C: Preterm neonates. E: Not the threshold.

questions.stem: In a preterm neonate without major bleeding, platelets are transfused below what level?
questions.explanation: Preterm neonates without major bleeding: transfuse at < 25 ×10⁹/L. B: Adults on chemotherapy. C: Major surgery. D: Lumbar puncture. E: Too high.

questions.stem: A woman with TTP has a platelet count of 9 ×10⁹/L and no bleeding. Why are platelets withheld?
questions.explanation: Avoid platelet transfusion in TTP and HIT, except for life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedures: platelet activation. A: Not the reason. B: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A patient with ALL receives leukocyte-depleted red cells. Which risk does leukocyte depletion lower?
questions.explanation: Leukocyte depletion: significant reduction in CMV transmission, WBC immunization and febrile reactions. A: Irradiation. B: Not affected. D: Volume-related. E: Plasma proteins.

questions.stem: Which cellular blood component is not leukocyte-depleted?
questions.explanation: All cellular blood components, except granulocyte concentrates, must be leukocyte depleted (< 5 ×10⁶ WBCs per component). B: Must be depleted. C: Must be depleted. D: Cellular; depleted. E: Must be depleted.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old on chemotherapy for ALL needs red cells. Which processing step stops donor T cells from dividing in him?
questions.explanation: Irradiation prevents donor T lymphocytes from dividing in the recipient and decreases GVHD. Indications include children on chemotherapy. A: Lowers CMV, immunization and fever. C: Antigen matching. D: Compatibility. E: Infections.

questions.stem: What does irradiation do to the shelf life of red cells?
questions.explanation: Irradiation decreases RBC shelf life to 28 days. A: Not the value. B: Not the value. C: Not the value. D: It is shortened.

questions.stem: Which patient needs irradiated blood products?

options.B: Adult with a bleeding peptic ulcer

questions.explanation: Irradiation: HSCT candidates and recipients, children on chemotherapy, primary immune deficiency, aplastic anemia on IST. B: Not listed. C: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which infection is part of the pretransfusion screen of donated blood?
questions.explanation: Infectious screen: HIV, HBV, HCV, HTLV and others. A: Not listed. B: Not listed. C: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A red cell unit has been out of the refrigerator for 45 minutes before the nurse is ready to start it. What should be done?
questions.explanation: Discard a pack that has been at room temperature > 4 h, out of the refrigerator > 30 min, opened, or shows signs of deterioration. A: Out of the fridge > 30 min. B: Out of the fridge > 30 min. C: Out of the fridge > 30 min. D: Out of the fridge > 30 min.

questions.stem: Before hanging a red cell unit, the nurse sees pink plasma above the red cells. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: Pink plasma means hemolysis: do not use. Any bag that fails a check is returned to the blood bank and never transfused. A: Milky plasma. B: The bag must not be used. D: Not the meaning. E: Look for large clots.

questions.stem: Which solution may run in the same tubing as a red cell unit?
questions.explanation: Only 0.9% sodium chloride, ABO-compatible plasma or albumin should be hung in the same tubing with a PRBC unit; avoid mixing medications with blood. A: Not allowed. C: Not allowed. D: No medications. E: No medications.

questions.stem: In adults, at what rate is a red cell unit started for the first 15 minutes?
questions.explanation: 1–2 mL/min (60–120 mL/h) for the first 15 minutes, then as rapidly as tolerated, not exceeding 4 hours. A: Too fast. B: Too fast. C: Too slow. E: Too fast.

questions.stem: A child with severe anemia shows signs of hypoxia. How much of the red cell transfusion is given quickly?
questions.explanation: Quickly give the first 5 mL/kg of PRBCs to relieve hypoxia, then slowly. If still critically low, give a second 5–10 mL/kg. B: Too much. C: Too little. D: Too much. E: The rest goes slowly.

questions.stem: For how long after a red cell transfusion is the patient monitored for reactions?

options.A: Up to 6 hours after it ends
options.B: Up to 30 min after it ends
options.C: Up to 24 hours after it ends
options.D: Up to 2 hours after it ends
options.E: Up to 12 hours after it ends

questions.explanation: Monitor the patient during transfusion and up to 30 minutes after its end: vital signs and signs of acute transfusion reactions. A: Not the value. C: Not the value. D: Not the value. E: Not the value.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative young woman needs a platelet transfusion and only Rh-positive platelets are available. What is the concern?

options.A: Hemolysis from anti-D in platelet plasma
options.E: Rh immunization from red cell stroma

questions.explanation: Platelets contain enough red cell stroma (membrane fragments) to stimulate Rh immunization. A: Not the concern. B: Not the concern. C: Not related to Rh. D: Not the concern.

questions.stem: A platelet transfusion should be completed within what time?
questions.explanation: Complete platelet infusion within 30 minutes (15–30 min). A: Red cells. B: Immunoglobulin. D: Not the value. E: Not the value.

questions.stem: A child becomes febrile, hypotensive and shaky with chills 5 minutes after a platelet transfusion starts. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Transfusion-transmitted infection is mostly reported with platelet transfusion (bacterial contamination): rapid fever, chills, hypo- or hypertension, septic shock. A: Benign; no shock. B: No fever; IgA deficiency. C: Respiratory picture. E: Hypertension, volume.

questions.stem: Bacterial contamination of a transfused unit is suspected. What confirms the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Culture of the blood pack confirms the diagnosis. A: Hemolysis. C: TRALI or TACO. D: Compatibility. E: Anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A patient has suspected bacterial contamination after a platelet transfusion. The transfusion is stopped and cultures are sent. What else is started promptly?
questions.explanation: Stop the transfusion, assess and stabilize, notify the blood bank, culture patient and bag, and start IV antibiotics promptly. A: Anaphylaxis. B: Urticarial reaction. D: AHTR. E: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into a red cell transfusion, a postpartum woman has fever, chills, flushing, dyspnea and red urine. BP 55/40 mmHg. PT and aPTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is high. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: AHTR: incompatible blood → recipient antibodies against donor antigens → intravascular hemolysis; fever, chills, flushing, dyspnea, back pain, red urine; DIC, shock, organ failure. A: No hemolysis or shock. B: Hives only. C: No red urine or DIC. D: Days to weeks later.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
questions.explanation: AHTR: commonest cause is infusion of incompatible (most likely ABO) blood due to clerical or nursing error. B: FNHTR. C: TRALI. D: Infection. E: Urticarial reaction.

questions.stem: A patient has an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. After the transfusion is stopped, which treatment is specific to this reaction?
questions.explanation: Treatment: AHTR, aggressive hydration and diuresis. ATR: epinephrine, steroids, vasopressors. UTR: antihistamines. FNHTR: antipyretics. TA-GVHD: steroids and immune suppressants. A: Anaphylaxis. B: Urticarial reaction. D: FNHTR. E: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with hereditary IgA deficiency receives plasma. Within minutes she has wheeze, stridor, hives and hypotension. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: ATR: most often in hereditary IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibody after IgA-containing products; wheezing, laryngeal edema and hypotension in severe cases. A: Hives without wheeze or hypotension. B: Fever, red urine. C: Pulmonary edema within 6 h. E: Fever, chills.

questions.stem: A woman has an anaphylactic transfusion reaction with stridor and hypotension. Which drug is given?
questions.explanation: ATR: epinephrine, steroids, vasopressors, respiratory support. A: Urticarial reaction. C: FNHTR. D: TACO. E: Infection.

questions.stem: Anaphylactic transfusion reactions are seen most often in patients with which condition?
questions.explanation: ATR: most often in patients with hereditary IgA deficiency who make anti-IgA antibody and then receive IgA-containing products. A: Not the risk group. B: Not the risk group. C: Not the risk group. D: Not the risk group.

questions.stem: Forty minutes into a red cell transfusion, a man develops itchy hives on one arm. Vital signs are normal and there is no wheeze. The transfusion is paused and an antihistamine given; he stays symptom-free for 30 minutes. What next?
questions.explanation: UTR: urticaria or itching within minutes; antihistamines, resume transfusion if no symptoms after 30 min. Permanent stop needs features such as hives over > 2/3 of the body. B: Localized hives allow resuming. C: Anaphylaxis. D: AHTR. E: Infection.

questions.stem: What causes urticarial transfusion reactions?

options.D: Recipient IgE against a donor protein
options.E: Recipient antibodies to donor red cells

questions.explanation: UTR: quite common; mostly caused by preformed recipient IgE antibody interacting with a donor allergen or protein. A: Anaphylactic reaction. B: FNHTR. C: TRALI. E: AHTR.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with iron deficiency anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding receives red cells. An hour in, she develops fever, chills and malaise; BP and urine are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: FNHTR: the most common reaction; fever, chills, malaise; a diagnosis of exclusion. A: No hypotension or red urine. B: No wheeze or hypotension. C: Respiratory signs. D: Days later.

questions.stem: What causes a febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.C: Recipient IgE against a donor protein
options.D: Donor T cells dividing in the host

questions.explanation: FNHTR is caused by cytokines released from donor leukocytes during storage; prevented by leukocyte filters. A: ATR. C: UTR. D: TA-GVHD. E: AHTR.

questions.stem: Which measure prevents febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions?
questions.explanation: FNHTR prevention: use of leukocyte filters. A: Prevents TA-GVHD. B: TACO. D: TACO. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which is the most common transfusion reaction?
questions.explanation: FNHTR is the most common transfusion reaction. B: Quite common. C: Rarer. D: Rarer. E: Rarer.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with AML has fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, pancytopenia and very high liver enzymes. Ten days ago he received a non-irradiated red cell unit at a small hospital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TA-GVHD: donor T lymphocytes in a host with weak immunity; fever, rash, diarrhea, vomiting, hepatic dysfunction and pancytopenia 10–30 days after transfusion. A: Rash, diarrhea and liver injury after transfusion point elsewhere. C: No rash or pancytopenia. D: Within hours. E: Within minutes.

questions.stem: Transfusion-associated graft versus host disease is fatal mostly because of what?
questions.explanation: TA-GVHD has a high fatality rate, mostly due to pancytopenia. B: Not the main cause. C: Not the main cause. D: Not the main cause. E: Not the main cause.

questions.stem: Which patient is at risk of transfusion-associated graft versus host disease?

options.E: An athlete with a femoral shaft fracture

questions.explanation: At risk: premature and LBW infants, children with PID, organ transplant recipients, patients on chemotherapy or IST. Prevented by irradiated products. A: Normal immunity. B: Normal immunity. D: Normal immunity. E: Normal immunity.

questions.stem: Two hours into a plasma transfusion, a patient develops sudden dyspnea, hypoxia and diffuse bilateral infiltrates. BP is 100/60 mmHg and the JVP is normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TRALI: sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, pulmonary edema and diffuse infiltrates within 6 h of any plasma-containing product. A: Hypertension, raised JVP. B: Wheeze, urticaria. C: Red urine. E: Fever without lung injury.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of TRALI?

options.A: Recipient antibodies against donor red cells
options.D: Donor T cells attacking the host

questions.explanation: TRALI: donor antibodies attack recipient WBCs and pulmonary endothelial cells, increasing pulmonary vascular permeability. A: AHTR. B: TACO. C: UTR. D: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with heart failure receives 3 red cell units rapidly. Four hours later he has dyspnea, BP 175/95 mmHg, raised JVP, basal crackles and frothy pink sputum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TACO: rapid large-volume transfusion → acute LVF and pulmonary edema within 12 h; hypertension, raised JVP, basal crackles, frothy pink sputum. B: Normal JVP; no hypertension. C: Hypotension, wheeze. D: Red urine, hypotension. E: Fever, chills.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old develops transfusion-associated circulatory overload. After stopping the transfusion, which drug is given?
questions.explanation: TACO management: stop the transfusion, give oxygen and diuretics, respiratory support as needed. A: Anaphylaxis. B: Urticarial reaction. C: FNHTR. E: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: What is the leading cause of transfusion-related death?
questions.explanation: TACO: leading cause (32% of fatalities). TRALI: second (21%). A: Second leading cause (21%). B: Less common. C: Rare. D: Less common.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with heart failure and chronic kidney disease needs two units of red cells. How should they be given?

options.B: Transfuse one unit at a time

questions.explanation: TACO prevention: transfuse one unit at a time, slow the rate, give a diuretic in patients at risk. A: Prevents TA-GVHD. C: Prevents FNHTR. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into a red cell transfusion, a patient develops fever and chills. What is the first step?
questions.explanation: First step: stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV open with 0.9% sodium chloride and see the patient. Early signs of benign and serious reactions are similar. A: Stop first. B: Stop first. D: Stop first. E: Stop first.

questions.stem: What is the cornerstone of preventing transfusion reactions?

options.C: Universal irradiation of red cell units
options.D: Routine use of fresh red cell units

questions.explanation: A restrictive attitude towards transfusion plus pretransfusion testing is the cornerstone of prevention. B: Not the cornerstone. C: Prevents TA-GVHD. D: Not needed. E: Not the cornerstone.

questions.stem: How should an acute transfusion reaction be regarded at its onset?

options.C: Febrile and harmless if vitals are stable
options.D: Infectious until cultures come back negative

questions.explanation: All acute transfusion reactions must be considered potentially serious until proved otherwise; early signs of benign and serious reactions may be similar. A: Early signs are similar. B: Not the rule. C: Not the rule. D: Not the rule.

questions.stem: Which finding means a transfusion must be stopped permanently?

options.D: A few hives on the chest

questions.explanation: Stop permanently: reaction < 15 min after starting, temperature > 39 °C, hypotension or shock, chills, back or chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia or arrhythmias, flushing or hives over > 2/3 of the body, hemoglobinuria, bleeding from the IV site. A: Mild; can resume. C: Below 39 °C. D: Below 2/3 of the body. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Why does chronic transfusion inevitably cause iron overload?

options.B: Donor red cells release free iron at once

questions.explanation: Iron overload: increased intake (transfusions) or increased absorption with normal intake. Humans have a limited ability to eliminate excess iron. A: Not the reason. B: Not the reason. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: Which condition causes iron overload mainly through increased intestinal absorption rather than transfusion?
questions.explanation: Non-transfusion (increased intestinal iron absorption): hereditary hemochromatosis and ineffective erythropoiesis (NTDT, sideroblastic anemia, CDA, MDS). A: Transfusion-related. B: Transfusion-related. C: Transfusion-related. E: Transfusion-related.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has fatigue, joint pain, raised liver enzymes, new diabetes and darkened skin. Transferrin saturation is 78% and ferritin 1,800 ng/mL; CRP is normal. Which genotype is most likely?
questions.explanation: HH is AR; homozygosity for C282Y in around 80%, compound heterozygosity C282Y/H63D, other HFE mutations, and less often non-HFE genes. The triad of cirrhosis, diabetes and skin pigmentation = "bronze diabetes". A: Less common. C: Less common. D: No iron overload. E: No iron overload.

questions.stem: On which chromosome is the HFE gene?
questions.explanation: HFE (type 1 HH) lies on the short arm of chromosome 6; inheritance is autosomal recessive. A: ABO. B: β-globin. C: α-globin. E: Not HFE.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of severe iron overload?
questions.explanation: Hereditary hemochromatosis is the most common cause of severe iron overload. A: Transfusion-related. B: Transfusion-related. C: Ineffective erythropoiesis. D: Less common.

questions.stem: How are most patients with hereditary hemochromatosis first identified?
questions.explanation: Most patients (75%) are asymptomatic and are diagnosed on routine chemistry or a positive family history. B: Classic triad, but late. C: Late. D: Late. E: Late.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has heart failure, hypogonadism and very high transferrin saturation. He has never been transfused. Which form of iron overload fits his age?
questions.explanation: HH usually presents at 40–50 years, except the juvenile form (10–30 years). Manifestations: cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, endocrinopathies, hyperpigmentation, HCC, arthropathy. A: Presents at 40–50 years. B: Never transfused. D: Not suggested. E: Never transfused.

questions.stem: Which transferrin saturation supports a diagnosis of hereditary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Labs: transferrin saturation ≥ 45%, serum ferritin ≥ 150–300 ng/mL without inflammation, high liver iron concentration. A: Too low. C: Too low. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A man is newly diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment: phlebotomy at frequent intervals until iron depletion; chelation; liver transplant for end-stage liver disease and HCC; arthroplasty for severe joint destruction. A: End-stage liver disease or HCC. B: Severe joint destruction. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: What is the goal of therapy in hereditary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Goal: remove iron before it produces irreversible parenchymal damage. Early diagnosis and iron depletion increase survival. B: Not the goal. C: Damage is irreversible. D: Wrong direction. E: Not the goal.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with hereditary hemochromatosis has end-stage cirrhosis and a small hepatocellular carcinoma. Which treatment addresses his liver disease?
questions.explanation: Liver transplantation is for end-stage liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma in HH. A: Iron depletion; not for end-stage disease. B: Joint destruction. C: Not listed. D: Adds iron.

questions.stem: A preterm newborn on a ventilator needs a red cell transfusion. Which modification of the unit prevents transfusion-associated graft versus host disease?
questions.explanation: TA-GVHD is prevented by irradiated blood products; premature and LBW infants are at risk. A: Lowers CMV, immunization and fever. B: Antigen matching. C: Not needed. E: TACO prevention.

questions.stem: Leukocyte depletion is applied selectively in a hospital. Which patient should receive leukocyte-depleted units?

options.A: A healthy adult having knee surgery
options.C: A young man after a car crash
options.E: An adult with a bleeding peptic ulcer

questions.explanation: Leukocyte depletion should be universal; if selective: infants and neonates, immune deficient patients, SCT recipients and oncology patients, chronically transfused patients. A: Not in the selective list. C: Not in the selective list. D: Not in the selective list. E: Not in the selective list.

questions.stem: A group A patient is given group B red cells by mistake. What destroys the donor red cells?
questions.explanation: AHTR: incompatible (most likely ABO) blood → recipient antibodies against donor antigens → intravascular hemolysis. A group A recipient has anti-B in plasma. A: Act on recipient cells. B: No A antigen on donor cells. C: TA-GVHD. D: Urticarial reaction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with β-thalassemia who has never been transfused has a high ferritin and liver iron. What is the mechanism of his iron overload?

options.A: Iron delivered by red cell transfusions

questions.explanation: Non-transfusion-related iron overload (increased intestinal absorption): hereditary hemochromatosis and ineffective erythropoiesis (NTDT, sideroblastic anemia, CDA, MDS). A: Never transfused. B: Not the cause in thalassemia. C: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.
